**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Bubbles are not proof. Neither is a colour change. This week you learn what actually counts as evidence that a new substance formed, and why mass that seems to disappear never really does.

1. Read **Did Anything New Actually Form?**
2. Learn the words in **Reaction Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Study the **Signs and Their Impostors** chart — it is the heart of the unit.
4. Trace **What Happens to the Atoms** before the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Chemical or Physical?**
6. Take **Reaction Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Two Rules**.
8. Read **Reaction Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Investigation: The Sealed Bag**.

Your job this week: catch one claim — an advert, a video, a classmate — that treats a sign as if it were proof. ⚗️

Picture panels: Identity and rearrangement; Clues need context; Everyday reaction examples; New solids and conserved atoms. Text-free illustrations use editable captions and image-specific descriptions. Diagrams simplify scale, anatomy and processes; colors and tokens are explained in captions. Follow the lesson text for scientific context. Educator review is pending.

## Did Anything New Actually Form?

Drop an antacid tablet in water and it fizzes furiously. Boil that same water and it bubbles just as hard. One of those is a chemical **reaction** and one is not. The bubbles cannot tell you which.

That is the problem this lesson solves.

A **substance** is a material with its own fixed **property** set: melting point, density, colour, how it reacts with other things. In a chemical reaction, the substances you start with — the **reactants** — are used up, and different substances — the **products** — appear in their place. In a **physical** change, no new substance appears. The same stuff has changed form.

Water boiling is physical. Steam is still water. Sugar dissolving is physical too, which surprises people, because the sugar vanishes from sight. Evaporate the water and the sugar comes back, unchanged. It was never destroyed, only spread out.

So what counts as evidence? Textbooks list five **indicators**: bubbles of gas, a colour change, a temperature change, light, and a **precipitate** — a solid appearing when two clear liquids mix.

Here is the part usually left out. **Every one of those five has a physical impostor.** Bubbles can be boiling. A colour change can be dilution. A temperature change can be dissolving, which warms or cools a solution without any reaction at all. Light can be an object glowing simply because it is hot. And a solid can appear because something merely suspended has settled out, with nothing new formed. Each indicator says *look closer*. None of them proves anything by itself.

The real test is the definition. Compare the properties before and after. If what you have at the end melts at a different temperature, or has a different density, or refuses to dissolve where the original dissolved easily, then you have different substances, and a reaction happened.

Now the second rule, and it is stranger.

Burn a log and the ash weighs far less than the wood. Mass looks lost. It is not. Carbon dioxide and water vapour left as gases, and nobody weighed them. Do the same burning inside a sealed container and the total mass does not budge.

That is because **atoms** are not created or destroyed in a reaction. They are rearranged. Every atom that goes in comes out, in some new arrangement, so mass is **conserved**. Antoine Lavoisier established this in the 1770s by insisting on sealed vessels and a good balance, which is a reminder that better measurement, not a better idea, settled it.

So ask two questions. Are the properties different now? And where did the atoms go?

## Did Anything New Actually Form?

A liquid fizzes. Did a reaction happen? Perhaps. Bubbles can also come from boiling or gas escaping from a drink. They show that gas is present, but not where it came from.

A chemical **reaction** forms new substances. Atoms rearrange and bonds change. **Reactants** are used in the change; **products** form. Some reactant may be left over. Some product may already be in the starting mixture.

A pure **substance** has a set chemical makeup. Its **properties**, such as density, help us study it. Conditions matter: the same material can have different density at a different temperature. A mixture can also behave differently from a pure substance.

In a **physical** change, the chemical identity stays the same. Boiling water is still water. When ordinary sugar dissolves in water, its molecules spread out but remain sugar. Getting the sugar back supports that account. Yet “can it be reversed?” is not a sure test. Some chemical reactions can go in both directions too.

Useful **indicators** include bubbles, color change, a change in temperature, light, and a solid appearing. A **precipitate** is a solid that separates from a solution. A reaction can form a new solid that does not dissolve.

Look for other explanations as well. Adding water can make a colored solution paler. Some physical mixing can warm or cool materials. A hot object may glow. Particles already in a liquid can settle. Crystals may appear as water leaves, without a new substance forming.

Use several observations and suitable tests. Compare materials under matched conditions. Does the evidence identify a new substance? Could temperature, concentration or an impurity explain the difference instead?

Now track the matter. When wood burns, it combines with oxygen from the air. Gases and ash form. We cannot compare only the wood and ash: that leaves out the oxygen that came in and gases that left.

In an ordinary chemical reaction, **atoms** of each element are **conserved**. They are not created or lost. In a closed system, no matter enters or leaves. Its mass stays the same at the precision of classroom tools. Count the same apparatus and all materials before and after. Check for leaks and measurement error if results differ.

Our colored tokens model atoms. The red and blue pairs are an invented counting example, not a real reaction or a recipe. The drawn boxes mark system boundaries, not containers to seal and heat. Use the model to ask where every atom went.

from: A temperature change is an indicator, not proof. Dissolving can warm or cool a solution with no reaction at all. They should compare the properties of what they have now with what they started with, such as melting point, density or solubility, and see whether a genuinely different substance is present.
to: Temperature change has multiple possible causes. Physical mixing or some dissolving can change temperature, while other dissolving involves reactions. Compare identified materials under matched conditions, using multiple tests and checking temperature, concentration and purity before concluding that a new substance formed.

from: Design a way to show that mass is conserved when baking soda reacts with vinegar. Explain why your setup works.
to: A teacher supplies data for a gas-forming reaction in open and closed systems. What must you compare to test conservation of mass?

from: Carry out the reaction in a sealed container, such as a closed bag or a stoppered flask, and weigh it before and after. The mass stays the same because the carbon dioxide produced cannot escape and is still on the balance. Doing it in an open beaker would appear to lose mass, because the gas leaves unweighed.
to: Compare the same complete system before and after, including apparatus, all reactants and all products. In the closed-system data the gas remains within the measured boundary, so the mass difference should be consistent with measurement uncertainty. In the open system some gas leaves that boundary. Analyze supplied data; do not seal a gas-producing reaction in a rigid container.

from: Usually yes. A raw egg turning solid is proteins changing shape and bonding differently, and you cannot get the raw egg back. Melting butter, though, is physical. Cooking is a mix of both.
to: Cooking can cause both kinds of change. Browning makes new substances. Melting changes state. Being hard to reverse does not, by itself, tell us which kind occurred.

from: Not in the same simple way. In nuclear changes a tiny amount of mass converts to energy, which is what E = mc squared describes. For every chemical reaction you will meet in this course, mass is conserved.
to: Nuclear changes need an account of both mass and energy. The tiny mass changes linked to energy transfers in ordinary chemistry are too small for classroom tools to detect. Nuclear changes can also change one element into another.

from: Oxygen in the air reacts with compounds in the fruit, helped along by an enzyme released when you cut the cells open. It is a genuine chemical reaction, which is why lemon juice slows it down.
to: Cutting damages cells. Oxygen, enzymes and other materials can then take part in browning reactions. Color alone would not identify a reaction in an unknown material.

from: Many can. Some run both ways at once and settle at a balance point. Others are practically one-way, like burning. Reversible does not mean easy to reverse.
to: Many reactions can run both ways. At equilibrium, the two directions proceed at the same rate. The amounts stay steady even though reactions continue.

from: Usually not, and this trips up everyone. Salt in water separates into the charged particles it is built from, and evaporating brings the salt back unchanged. Some dissolvings do involve reactions, so the recovery test is the one to trust.
to: It depends on the materials. Sugar molecules stay sugar when they dissolve in water. Other materials can react as they dissolve. Check what substances are present.

from: By weighing very carefully in sealed vessels. Lavoisier could not see an atom, but he could show that closed systems do not change mass. Good measurement settled it long before good microscopes existed.
to: They made careful mass measurements while tracking matter that entered or left. A balanced equation also accounts for each kind of atom. Small measurement differences need to be checked against the limits of the tools.
